deep.reconstruction:
Page 71 is the last page of the 1983 Teichmüller notes. It is a title, 'découpages pantalonesques d'une carte (triangulée)' (pants decompositions attached to a triangulated map), plus two drawings and no text argument.

Left drawing. A graphite graph, a 'carte' drawn on the plane/sphere, has about 11 vertices, each with a small brown circle around it. Some edges run off to infinity. The small circles are the boundary curves around the punctures if the vertices are treated as marked points. Around them is a family of nested closed brown curves, drawn like contour lines on a topographic map (an evident pun on 'carte').
- The innermost curve encloses two vertices joined by an edge. Each successive curve encloses one or a few more vertices, until the outermost curve encloses all of them.
- Each brown curve carries small dots where it crosses the edges of the map. So the curves are drawn transverse to the map, and their intersection numbers with the edges are being recorded.
- On a sphere with n marked points, a nested chain enclosing 2, 3, ..., n−2 points is a pants decomposition (n−3 curves) of 'comb' or caterpillar type. More generally a nested system of contour curves, i.e. the level sets of a function on the vertices / a sweep-out, cuts out a pants decomposition.
- So the left picture shows a way to produce pants decompositions of the punctured surface from the combinatorial map: order or filter the vertices and draw contours around growing sets of them.

Right drawing. A trivalent graph with a few dangling half-edges (the boundary components) and one loop at a vertex, so the surface has genus ≥ 1. This is the dual graph of a pants decomposition: vertices are pairs of pants, edges are cutting curves, the loop is a one-holed torus.
- Small integers sit at the ends of the edges near each trivalent vertex (e.g. 1,5,4; 4,4,2; 2,5,1; 4,2,3; 3,3,17 or similar).
- Larger bold numbers (15, 19, 17, 1, 7?) sit at some vertices, and a few edges carry circled indices 1, 2, 3.
- The most plausible reading: the half-edge numbers are combinatorial data of the map relative to the decomposition. They would be intersection numbers of the map's edges with the cutting curves (the normal / Dehn–Thurston-type coordinates of the map's 1-skeleton relative to the pants decomposition). The bold vertex numbers would then be counts of map elements (vertices, edges or triangles) inside each pair of pants. The circled numbers may index curves or an order of cutting.
- Parity checks such as 1+5+4 and 4+4+2 being even are consistent with intersection numbers of arcs in a pair of pants. Some triples, e.g. 3+3+7 if read correctly, are not. So the reading is uncertain.

Purpose. The previous page defines the topological Teichmüller groupoids (oriented, bi-oriented, 'divisé' variants with a 1-dimensional submanifold Σ and marked points). This page sketches the bridge between those groupoids and combinatorial maps (dessins/triangulations): a map determines a family of pants decompositions, i.e. base points/vertices in the 'Lego' presentation of the Teichmüller groupoid. These are encoded combinatorially by intersection data with the map. This is the program later announced in Esquisse d'un programme (1984): Teichmüller tower generated by pants decompositions, linked to 'cartes' and dessins d'enfants.
errors: No explicit claims to check. Some half-edge triples in the right diagram (e.g. 3,3,7 at the upper-right vertex, if read correctly) violate the parity condition (sum of intersection numbers at a pair of pants must be even) that intersection numbers of a closed transverse 1-complex... would satisfy only if the numbers are intersection numbers of arcs; so either the reading is wrong, the numbers mean something else (counts of vertices/edges), or there is a slip.

The left drawing shows more nested curves than strictly needed in places (curves enclosing the same set of punctures would be isotopic and redundant). This is consistent with a 'contour map' sketch rather than a minimal pants decomposition.

missed.claim: A combinatorial map (dessin/triangulation) on a surface canonically determines a family of pants decompositions, via nested 'contour' curves transverse to the map, together with intersection data. This would give a direct bridge from the Grothendieck–Teichmüller action on dessins to the Lego/pants presentation of the Teichmüller groupoid. The thread stops here, the last page of the notes; the specific map→pants-decomposition construction with intersection labels does not seem to be developed in the later dessins/GT literature.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: A combinatorial dictionary between dessins (on which Gal(Q̄/Q) acts) and pants coordinates (where the GT relations live) could make Galois actions on dessins computable in Dehn–Thurston-type coordinates. That link is mostly treated separately in the literature.

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a sketch: a pants decomposition drawn as contour lines around the vertices of a map, plus a labelled dual trivalent graph. Pants decompositions linked to maps are the familiar Esquisse program. The only mildly notable point is the specific idea of extracting pants decompositions from a triangulated map by nested level curves, with intersection labels. It is undeveloped and too fragmentary to count as a result.
transcription_corrections: Title is 'découpages pantalonesques / d'une carte (triangulée)' — confirmed.
In the right diagram the bold '1 9' near the top vertex may be a single bold '19' (vertex total) rather than two separate labels.
The label read as '7' at the upper-right vertex may be a '+' or '7'; uncertain.
The edge leaving the vertex labelled 2,1,5 ends in an arrowhead (a marked/oriented boundary end), not just a plain edge.
Bold '15' and '17' are vertex labels (attached to vertices), distinct from the small half-edge numbers; the circled 1, 2, 3 are separate indices on edges.
Left drawing: about 11 vertices are individually circled in brown (small boundary loops), and about 8–10 nested brown contour curves have dots marking crossings with the graphite edges.
